# Piston pumps (suction and force pump) (`piston_pump`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by atmospheric_pressure, lathe_screw_cutting, boring_machine
- Core idea: A piston slides in a smooth barrel; two one-way flap valves do the rest. In the suction (lift) pump a foot valve sits at the bottom of the barrel and a second valve in the piston itself: raising the piston lets the air's pressure push water up the pipe, lowering it passes the water through the piston, and the next stroke lifts it out. The pump can stand no more than about 7 to 8 m above the water (10.3 m is the ideal head at sea level; altitude, warm water and flow losses reduce it). In the force pump a solid piston draws water through an inlet check valve on one stroke. On the return stroke that valve shuts and a delivery check opens into the rising main. Delivery head depends on the force available and the pressure the barrel and joints can bear. The piston is sealed with a leather cup or greased hemp; the barrel is bored elm, cast bronze or iron. Deep mines use several lifts in series, each within suction height of a cistern.
- Pitfalls:
  - Believing suction can raise water from any depth; above about 10 m the column breaks (and in practice well before)
  - Air leaks on the suction side, a dry leather or no priming: the pump moves air, not water
  - A rough or tapering barrel; the piston seal must fit along the whole stroke
  - Lead barrels and pipes for drinking water
- History: greece: c. 270 BC – Ctesibius of Alexandria, two-cylinder bronze force pump (in Vitruvius and Hero); rome: 1st–4th c. AD – bronze and wooden force pumps for fire fighting, wells and bilges (finds at Silchester and Bolsena); china: piston bellows and syringes old, and the square-pallet chain pump from the 1st c. AD (Wang Chong, c. 80); the piston water pump only arrives with the Jesuits (Taixi shuifa, 1612); islamic: 1206 – al-Jazari's water-driven twin-cylinder pump with true suction pipes; 1551 Taqi al-Din's six-cylinder pump; europe: c. 1433–1450 – Taccola draws the suction lift pump with a valved piston; 1556 Agricola shows mine pumps in series; 1640s the 10 m limit explained by air pressure
- Read:
  - Vitruvius, De architectura X.7
  - Sheldon Shapiro, The Origin of the Suction Pump, Technology and Culture 5 (1964)
  - John Peter Oleson, Greek and Roman Mechanical Water-Lifting Devices: The History of a Technology (1984)
